EXPERIMENT: Two models will be trained on matched datasets: (1) baseline model on chemical structures alone (ChEMBL v32 + ZINC20 SMILES), and (2) multi-modal model incorporating Nigerian medicinal plant genomics and metabolomics data (from Nigerian Natural Medicine Database and GNPS) alongside chemical data. Generated molecules will be evaluated for predicted bioactivity against *Trypanosoma cruzi* and *Leishmania donovani* using an independent QSAR predictor trained on unseen TDR Targets Database bioassays, and scaffold novelty will be quantified by Tanimoto similarity against known actives. Statistical significance of at least 0.5 log unit increase in predicted pIC50 and 20% uplift in scaffold novelty (p < 0.05) will validate the hypothesis; failure to achieve these metrics will falsify it. Additional intermediate models (chemical + genomics only, chemical + metabolomics only) and plans for synthesizing and experimentally testing top candidates will further disentangle modality contributions and confirm translational relevance.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates multi-modal indigenous Nigerian plant omics data with global chemical datasets in a unified generative AI framework, leveraging graph-based biosynthetic gene cluster embeddings and spectral metabolomics fingerprints conditioned on NTD bioactivity. Unlike prior studies that focus on chemical structures alone or general natural products, our approach exploits rich biological context from underrepresented local biodiversity, supported by rigorous data preprocessing, modality ablation controls, and planned experimental validation, thereby advancing multi-modal generative modeling for neglected disease drug discovery.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
In heterogeneous federated learning, personalized data augmentation strategies tailored to each client’s local data distribution reduce client drift and improve global model accuracy more effectively than global knowledge distillation alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning with heterogeneous, non-IID client data suffers from client drift, where local model updates diverge due to varying distributions, slowing global convergence and degrading performance. Existing methods like global knowledge distillation guide local training via a global teacher but do not explicitly address distribution mismatch at the client level. Effective mitigation of client drift remains an open problem critical for reliable federated learning in real-world diverse settings.

APPROACH:  
We propose dynamically selecting personalized augmentation policies for each client based on its local data class imbalance and feature statistics, using a predefined augmentation pool (e.g., rotation, color jitter, cutout, mixup) optimized to balance class representation and enhance feature generalization per client. This personalized augmentation is periodically updated during training without relying on global knowledge distillation, aiming to align local training distributions with global expectations and reduce gradient variance. We also conduct ablations combining personalized augmentation with knowledge distillation and generic augmentation to isolate the benefits of personalization.

EXPERIMENT:  
We simulate 50 clients on FEMNIST and CIFAR-10-LT datasets partitioned to reflect realistic non-IID heterogeneity, comparing FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, global knowledge distillation (GKD), generic augmentation, personalized augmentation (PA), and PA+GKD across 200 communication rounds. Evaluation metrics include average global test accuracy, per-client accuracy variance (to measure client drift), and convergence speed (rounds to 90% final accuracy), with statistical significance verified over multiple runs. Success requires PA to outperform GKD by ≥2% in global accuracy and reduce client variance by ≥10%, demonstrating superior client drift mitigation.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work relying solely on global teacher guidance, this approach introduces a theoretically motivated, data-driven augmentation policy selection mechanism personalized per client to directly address local distribution shifts and class imbalance. The comprehensive experimental design—including ablations and rigorous statistical evaluation—clarifies the causal impact of personalization and its synergy with knowledge distillation, advancing the understanding of heterogeneity-aware federated learning.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating personalized meta-learning adapter layers on top of federated models mitigates client-drift more effectively than control variate methods like SCAFFOLD in highly non-IID and heterogeneous federated learning settings.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning suffers from client-drift when local updates on heterogeneous, non-IID data cause local models to diverge, slowing convergence and degrading global model performance. Existing approaches like SCAFFOLD address drift via control variates applied globally, but often fail to sufficiently personalize models for diverse clients or scale well under asynchronous participation. Effective personalization that balances adaptation and drift mitigation remains an open challenge, especially for real-world federated datasets with intrinsic client heterogeneity.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting a shared global federated model with lightweight, client-specific meta-learning adapter layers trained via a Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) procedure during local updates. Clients perform nested meta-train steps to update the global base model followed by meta-test steps to adapt their personalized adapter layers, which remain local and are not aggregated, enabling fast, stable adaptation to client-specific distributions without increasing global update variance. This contrasts with SCAFFOLD’s full-model control variates by isolating personalization in small meta-layers, improving drift mitigation and convergence in asynchronous and partial client participation scenarios.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on LEAF benchmark datasets FEMNIST and Sent140, comparing FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, and our personalized meta-learning model using global accuracy, per-client accuracy variance, rounds-to-90%-final-accuracy, and drift-specific metrics such as gradient variance and parameter divergence. To confirm the hypothesis, our method must outperform SCAFFOLD by at least +3% global accuracy, reduce per-client accuracy variance by 20%, and converge in fewer than 80% of SCAFFOLD’s communication rounds, with significance tested at p ≤ 0.05. Additional baselines include FedPer, Per-FedAvg, and local fine-tuning ablations to isolate meta-layer contributions.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies personalization or drift correction to entire local models, our method uniquely integrates MAML-style meta-learning adapter layers for federated personalization that simultaneously reduces client-drift by decoupling local adaptation from global aggregation. We provide a scalable, stability-validated nested optimization procedure suitable for asynchronous federated settings, along with comprehensive drift-specific metrics and ablations to clarify personalization versus drift mitigation contributions.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
Introducing a rigorously defined adaptive client grouping strategy based on multi-modal similarity metrics of client data distributions and model update statistics, combined with hierarchical aggregation and dynamic regrouping schedules, reduces the communication rounds needed for convergence in federated learning on heterogeneous, non-IID datasets compared to structured random grouping and state-of-the-art baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning on heterogeneous, non-IID data suffers from client drift and slow convergence due to diverse local data distributions causing model inconsistency. Existing methods like FedAvg and SCAFFOLD partially address these issues but do not explicitly leverage structured client grouping to align similar data distributions. There is a lack of thorough investigation into how adaptive, similarity-based grouping combined with hierarchical aggregation impacts convergence speed and model accuracy under realistic FL constraints.

APPROACH:  
Clients’ local data characteristics are represented by a combination of normalized label histograms and statistical embeddings derived from local model updates to capture richer heterogeneity. Clients are dynamically clustered using a hybrid similarity metric (e.g., weighted cosine similarity) and hierarchical clustering algorithms, with pre-defined regrouping intervals whose overhead is quantified and included in convergence metrics. During training, hierarchical aggregation occurs first within groups to reduce client drift, then globally, under synchronous federated rounds with fixed client participation. A structured random grouping baseline—random groups of equal size with hierarchical aggregation—is included to isolate the effect of similarity-based grouping from hierarchical aggregation itself.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate on CIFAR-10 (non-IID label-skew partitions with 2-3 classes per client) and FEMNIST (natural writer-based partitions) datasets by measuring the number of communication rounds to reach target accuracies (75% for CIFAR-10, 85% for FEMNIST), final model accuracy, and communication overhead including regrouping costs. Perform multiple independent runs with statistical tests (e.g., paired t-tests, confidence intervals) to validate significant convergence speedups (>20% reduction in rounds) without more than 5% accuracy loss compared to FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, and structured random grouping baselines.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates multi-modal client similarity metrics to improve grouping quality beyond simple label histograms, rigorously defines dynamic regrouping policies with overhead accounting, and empirically separates the benefits of similarity-based grouping from hierarchical aggregation. It also provides theoretical insights on convergence behavior under hierarchical grouping and analyzes robustness against noisy client data distribution estimates, distinguishing it from prior clustered or personalized federated learning methods.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating personalized meta-learning layers atop a shared global federated model reduces client-drift more effectively than global knowledge distillation for heterogeneous non-IID data by enabling fast local adaptation without increasing communication overhead.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning on heterogeneous, non-IID client data suffers from client-drift, where local updates diverge and slow global convergence or degrade performance. Existing drift-mitigation techniques like global knowledge distillation regularize local models towards a global teacher but often fail to capture client-specific nuances, limiting personalization and convergence speed. A method that enables efficient local adaptation while preserving a shared backbone is needed to better address client heterogeneity.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting FedAvg with small personalized meta-learning layers (e.g., fully connected modules) on top of a frozen global backbone, where clients adapt only these layers via Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML)-style inner-loop updates on local data each round. The global backbone is trained conventionally via FedAvg, while personalized layers remain local and allow client-specific feature refinement, reducing client-drift without increasing communicated model size or rounds.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on LEAF benchmark datasets FEMNIST (image) and Sent140 (text), both exhibiting strong non-IID user partitions, comparing FedAvg baseline, Local-Global Knowledge Distillation (LGKD), and our Personalized Meta-Learning Layers (PMLL) approach. Metrics include average and worst-case per-client test accuracy, test loss, convergence speed (communication rounds to target accuracy), and detailed measurement of communication and computational overhead. Ablations include local fine-tuning and multi-task personalization baselines to isolate meta-learning effects.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work relying on global teacher regularization or fine-tuning, our method uniquely combines meta-learned personalization layers with federated backbone training, enabling fast client-specific adaptation that mitigates client-drift more effectively and efficiently. This approach is validated across modalities with rigorous overhead quantification and comprehensive baselines, offering a theoretically grounded and practically deployable solution for heterogeneous federated learning.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating dynamically updated personalized adapter modules alongside a shared global backbone in federated learning reduces client-drift more effectively than static global-to-local knowledge distillation in heterogeneous non-IID settings.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning on heterogeneous and strongly non-IID client data suffers from client-drift, where local models diverge due to data distribution shifts, slowing convergence and reducing global accuracy. Existing methods like static local-global knowledge distillation regularize local training towards a fixed global teacher but lack mechanisms to continuously adapt client models to their evolving data distributions. Addressing this gap is critical for improving personalization and convergence in federated systems with natural client heterogeneity.

APPROACH: We propose Dynamic Personalized Component Federated Learning (DPC-FL), which augments a shared global CNN backbone with lightweight client-specific adapter modules (e.g., residual blocks or attention layers) that are initialized once and updated dynamically each communication round to adapt locally to data shifts. The global backbone parameters are aggregated via FedAvg, while personalized adapters remain client-local and adapt continuously, allowing direct model personalization beyond static regularization. This hybrid update scheme contrasts with Static Local-Global Knowledge Distillation (SLG-KD), where clients receive fixed global teacher knowledge as a distillation loss without personalized modules.

EXPERIMENT: We conduct controlled experiments on the LEAF FEMNIST dataset and CIFAR-10 partitioned by Dirichlet distribution (α=0.1) across 100 clients, training both DPC-FL and SLG-KD for 200 rounds under identical FedAvg settings. We compare global test accuracy, per-client accuracy variance, and convergence speed (communication rounds to 80% peak accuracy), performing statistical significance testing and ablation studies on adapter update frequency and initialization to validate the impact of dynamic personalization.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior personalized FL methods and static knowledge distillation approaches, DPC-FL introduces a rigorously defined, dynamically updated client adapter mechanism that explicitly tracks and adapts to client data distribution shifts each round, theoretically and empirically mitigating client-drift more effectively. This framework is systematically evaluated with comprehensive ablations, multiple heterogeneity levels, and robustness metrics, clarifying when and why dynamic personalization outperforms static regularization in heterogeneous federated learning.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained on multi-model CMIP6 climate simulation ensembles will generalize more robustly to unseen climate regimes and models than emulators trained on individual GCM data alone, as demonstrated by lower out-of-sample prediction error and improved physical consistency on excluded GCM datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate and efficient emulation of subgrid-scale processes is critical for accelerating climate model simulations, yet current deep learning emulators often fail to generalize beyond the training model or climate regime. Existing approaches typically train on a single GCM’s data, limiting their applicability across diverse climate conditions and model physics. This work addresses the challenge of developing emulators that transfer reliably to unseen climate states and models, enhancing robustness and utility for climate projections.

APPROACH:  
We propose training convolutional recurrent neural network (ConvRNN) emulators on pooled subgrid-scale outputs from multiple CMIP6 GCMs (CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, UKESM1) using domain adaptation techniques—including model-specific input embeddings and batch normalization—to capture shared physical patterns while accounting for inter-model biases. These multi-model emulators will be compared against single-model ConvRNN emulators and standard physics-based parameterizations, evaluating their ability to predict subgrid variables conditioned on coarse climate states.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate out-of-sample generalization by testing on GFDL-CM4 simulations excluded from training, quantifying predictive performance via mean squared error (MSE), explained variance score, and temporal autocorrelation metrics. Training and evaluation protocols will be rigorously standardized with matched architectures, hyperparameter optimization, and training budgets, while coverage of climate regimes in training data will be quantified and stratified to ensure representativeness. Statistical testing with confidence intervals and power analysis will determine if the multi-model emulator achieves at least 10% lower MSE on GFDL-CM4 data compared to the best single-model emulator.

NOVELTY:  
This work innovates by systematically leveraging CMIP6 multi-model ensembles to train deep learning emulators that learn shared, transferable representations of subgrid physics, combined with rigorous domain adaptation and evaluation strategies. Unlike prior single-model or physics-only approaches, it provides a theoretically grounded, statistically robust demonstration that multi-model training improves emulator generalization to previously unseen models and climate regimes, thereby advancing the practical integration of machine-learned emulators into climate modeling workflows.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained on multi-model CMIP6 climate ensembles with domain adversarial training will generalize more accurately to unseen climate regimes and extreme events than single-model emulators by learning model-invariant representations that mitigate structural biases across Earth System Models.

BACKGROUND:  
Current deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration often struggle to generalize beyond the climate regimes represented in single-model training data, limiting their reliability for predicting extreme events under future scenarios. Structural biases and shared dependencies among CMIP6 Earth System Models (ESMs) further constrain the effective diversity leveraged by multi-model training, necessitating approaches that explicitly address domain shifts. Robust evaluation of emulator skill on rare extremes remains challenging due to inadequate metrics sensitive to tail behavior.

APPROACH:  
We propose training convolutional LSTM-based emulators on concatenated multi-model CMIP6 outputs enriched with domain adversarial training (DAT) to enforce extraction of model-invariant features, thereby improving generalization to held-out climate models and scenarios with shifted extremes. Structural biases and inter-model dependencies will be characterized using statistical divergence measures and mitigated through adaptive sample weighting and physics-informed regularization during training. Emulator performance will be rigorously evaluated using a suite of tailored metrics including RMSE, continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, and extreme value theory-based tail indices to capture distributional shifts in heatwaves and heavy precipitation events.

EXPERIMENT:  
Training data will comprise daily high-resolution outputs of temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture from a subset of CMIP6 ESMs’ historical and SSP2-4.5 scenario runs; evaluation will use held-out models and SSP5-8.5 scenario outputs to test generalization on extreme event prediction. Baselines include single-model deep learning emulators trained conventionally, state-of-the-art statistical downscaling and bias-correction methods applied per model, and a multi-model emulator without DAT. Cross-model validation will leave one model out to quantify transferability. Success requires the DAT-enhanced multi-model emulator to reduce average RMSE by ≥15% and achieve statistically significant (p < 0.05) improvements in CRPS and tail metrics relative to the best single-model baseline.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously integrates domain adversarial training tailored to climate model ensembles to overcome structural biases and domain shifts among CMIP6 models, providing theoretical justification and mitigation strategies for inter-model dependencies rarely addressed in prior emulation studies. It uniquely combines advanced tail-sensitive evaluation grounded in extreme value theory with multi-model deep learning emulation for extreme event prediction, marking a substantive advance beyond existing single-model or naive multi-model approaches.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained on harmonized multi-model CMIP6 climate simulation ensembles will generalize significantly better to unseen and extreme climate regimes than emulators trained on single-model outputs, as demonstrated through rigorous out-of-sample testing against independent ESMs and abrupt forcing scenarios.

BACKGROUND:  
Current climate model emulators often rely on data from single Earth system models (ESMs), limiting their robustness and transferability when deployed on novel climate states or models. This restricts their utility for accelerating climate simulations under future extreme scenarios, where generalization beyond training distributions is critical. Addressing this gap requires systematically evaluating whether multi-model training improves emulator performance and reliability on out-of-sample climate regimes.

APPROACH:  
We will develop convolutional recurrent neural network (ConvRNN) emulators trained on harmonized, bias-corrected, and unit-standardized multi-model CMIP6 datasets, including outputs from at least five distinct ESMs (CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, GFDL-ESM4, UKESM1-0-LL, CanESM5). Parallel single-model ConvRNN emulators will be trained on each model’s output independently with matched network capacities and hyperparameters to isolate the effect of training data diversity. Emulators predict subgrid-scale fluxes from coarse-scale variables over historical and scenario runs (ssp370, ssp585).

EXPERIMENT:  
Generalization will be quantitatively evaluated by testing all emulators on out-of-sample CMIP6 models excluded from training (e.g., NorESM2-LM, MIROC6) and on abrupt 4xCO2 forcing experiments representing extreme climate regimes. Metrics include root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) against high-resolution reference outputs, with statistical significance assessed via bootstrapped confidence intervals and paired t-tests (p < 0.05). Success is defined as multi-model emulators achieving at least 10% lower RMSE and 0.1 higher R² compared to all single-model baselines.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates comprehensive data harmonization across multiple CMIP6 ESMs and enforces strict architectural parity to rigorously isolate the advantage of multi-model training for emulator generalization. Unlike prior studies limited to single-model training or physics-inspired emulators, it provides a robust, statistically grounded evaluation on truly novel climate regimes and extreme forcing scenarios, offering practical insights into emulator transferability for climate model acceleration.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Deep learning emulators trained on carefully harmonized multi-model CMIP6 ensembles with domain adaptation techniques generalize more robustly to diverse unseen climate regimes than emulators trained on single-model datasets.

BACKGROUND: Climate model emulators accelerate computationally expensive simulations but often struggle to generalize across different climate models and regimes due to inter-model biases and domain shifts. Existing emulators typically train on single climate models, limiting their applicability in broader climate prediction tasks, especially under novel future scenarios not represented in training data.

APPROACH: We develop convolutional LSTM emulators trained on pooled multi-model CMIP6 data from at least five distinct global climate models (CESM2, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, IPSL-CM6A-LR, UKESM1-0-LL, GFDL-CM4), incorporating domain adaptation layers and model-specific bias correction embeddings to reconcile inter-model heterogeneity. These emulators predict monthly spatiotemporal climate fields (temperature, precipitation, atmospheric circulation) given historical states and forcing parameters, with rigorous early stopping and hyperparameter tuning on dedicated multi-model validation sets.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate generalization by testing both the multi-model and single-model emulators on multiple independent, unseen CMIP6 models (including NorESM2-LM and additional hold-out models) under future SSP5-8.5 scenarios, using normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) and spatial pattern correlation as quantitative metrics. Statistical significance of performance differences will be assessed via bootstrap resampling, with the hypothesis falsified if the multi-model emulator fails to exceed the single-model baseline by at least 10% lower NRMSE and 5% higher spatial correlation on unseen models.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior single-model or non-adaptive multi-model emulators, this work explicitly addresses inter-model biases with domain adaptation and model embeddings, rigorously evaluates generalization across multiple unseen climate regimes, and provides a theoretically grounded framework connecting multi-model training to improved cross-regime robustness, advancing both emulator methodology and climate model interoperability.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
To test the hypothesis that deep learning emulators trained on multi-model ensemble outputs generalize better to unseen climate regimes than those trained on a single climate model’s data, we propose an experiment leveraging publicly available CMIP6 datasets. Specifically, we will use output variables related to subgrid-scale turbulent processes—such as temperature, humidity, and velocity fields—from multiple Earth System Models (ESMs), including CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, and HadGEM3-GC31. These datasets provide consistent variables across models and cover historical and future climate scenarios (ssp245 and ssp585), allowing testing on out-of-distribution (OOD) climates. The multi-model training dataset will combine all three models’ outputs, while single-model training datasets will use only one model’s data at a time.

Our baseline models will be deep neural networks (DNNs) trained to emulate subgrid-scale parameterizations (e.g., turbulent viscosity and diffusivity) following the architecture used in the 2020 study “Deep Learning Emulation of Subgrid‐Scale Processes in Turbulent Shear Flows”: a feedforward network taking as input resolved-scale variables (velocities, strain rates, density gradients) and outputting SGS coefficients. We will train one DNN per single-model dataset and one DNN on the combined multi-model dataset. We will evaluate all models on held-out data from unseen climate regimes—specifically, future climate projections and the outputs of a held-out ESM (e.g., training on CESM2 and MPI-ESM1.2 and testing on HadGEM3-GC31).

Quantitatively, success will be measured by the root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) between the predicted SGS parameters and the ground truth across the unseen regimes. A threshold for success is defined as the multi-model trained DNN achieving at least a 10% lower RMSE and 0.05 higher R² on the held-out data compared to the best single-model DNN. If the multi-model DNN’s performance is statistically indistinguishable (e.g., within 2 standard deviations) or worse on these metrics, the hypothesis is falsified.

Technically, the DNNs will be implemented with input normalization per model to accommodate distributional differences. Training uses Adam optimizer with early stopping based on validation loss within the training models’ domain. To handle multi-model data heterogeneity, we will explore domain-adversarial training or feature-wise normalization layers conditioned on the input model identity, to promote domain-invariant feature extraction. Testing on the unseen model’s data will reveal how well learned features generalize. If the multi-model DNN fails to outperform single-model counterparts on the held-out climate regime, this will falsify the hypothesis, indicating that multi-model training does not improve emulator generalizability in this context.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating neural architecture search (NAS) explicitly optimized for uncertainty calibration metrics such as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) within a computationally efficient NAS loop will produce deep neural networks with significantly better uncertainty quantification on out-of-distribution (OOD) data than ensembles or Bayesian methods matched for capacity and training budget.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks often exhibit overconfident predictions, especially on OOD inputs, limiting their deployment in safety-critical applications. While Bayesian methods and ensembles improve uncertainty estimates, they are computationally expensive and do not explicitly optimize architecture for calibration. A gap remains in designing architectures that inherently improve uncertainty calibration, particularly under distributional shifts.

APPROACH: We propose to integrate a calibration-aware NAS framework that uses a differentiable proxy for ECE, combined with batch-wise Monte Carlo estimation, to efficiently optimize network architectures for uncertainty calibration within the NAS loop. This approach assumes no OOD data during training but uses in-distribution calibration metrics as surrogates. The resulting architectures will be trained with standard methods and compared against ensembles and Bayesian networks with equivalent parameter counts and identical training protocols.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate on CIFAR-10/100 with established OOD benchmarks such as CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C (corrupted variants), and SVHN datasets, using metrics including ECE, negative log-likelihood (NLL), and OOD detection AUC. Baselines include deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, and Bayesian Neural Networks (e.g., Bayes By Backprop), all carefully hyperparameter-tuned to match the training budget and model size.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on post-hoc uncertainty estimation or Bayesian formulation, this study is the first to explicitly optimize neural architectures for calibration during the NAS process with rigorous computational strategies. It clarifies theoretical assumptions linking architecture design to calibration performance and provides a standardized, controlled OOD evaluation protocol to validate improvements beyond existing methods.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporate domain-specific causal structure priors into Bayesian uncertainty quantification frameworks for deep neural networks to reduce predictive uncertainty more effectively than standard Bayesian methods in high-stakes medical diagnosis tasks.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks deployed in critical applications such as medical diagnosis require reliable uncertainty estimates to support safe decision-making. Existing Bayesian UQ methods (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, variational Bayesian neural networks) quantify uncertainty statistically but do not leverage known causal relationships in clinical data, potentially limiting calibration and confidence. Integrating causal domain knowledge into UQ remains an open problem for improving uncertainty quality and clinical trustworthiness.

APPROACH: We propose embedding structured causal priors—derived from expert-validated directed acyclic graphs encoding relationships among symptoms, biomarkers, and diseases—directly into the Bayesian inference procedure of deep neural networks via probabilistic programming frameworks (e.g., Pyro). This causal prior constrains the posterior over network weights or latent variables to reflect domain causal dependencies, thereby informing uncertainty estimates to better reflect clinically meaningful relationships and reduce spurious uncertainty.

EXPERIMENT: Using the MIMIC-IV EHR dataset and the UK Biobank cardiovascular imaging/genetics dataset, we will evaluate the proposed causal-structured Bayesian UQ model against matched-architecture baselines implementing Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and variational Bayesian neural networks without causal priors. Performance will be measured on held-out clinical outcome prediction tasks by calibration (Expected Calibration Error), sharpness (negative log-likelihood, Brier score), and statistical significance (p < 0.05 with multiple comparison corrections) across multiple random seeds. Success requires at least a 15% relative reduction in ECE and significant improvements in NLL and Brier score over all baselines on both datasets; failure to meet this across all metrics falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies generic Bayesian UQ or causal inference separately, this approach formally integrates expert-curated causal graphs as structured priors within Bayesian neural network training, theoretically grounding how causal dependencies guide uncertainty estimation and demonstrating robustness to causal graph misspecification. This structured integration of domain causal knowledge into deep learning UQ in real-world, multi-modal clinical datasets represents a novel step towards clinically actionable uncertainty quantification.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Training deep neural networks with uncertainty-aware data augmentation, where the magnitude and frequency of input perturbations are adaptively weighted by model uncertainty estimates during training, leads to significantly improved calibration of predictive uncertainty compared to standard augmentation and other adaptive schemes.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks remains a critical challenge, especially in domains requiring reliable confidence estimates under distributional shifts or input corruptions. While methods such as MC-Dropout and ensembles improve uncertainty estimation, they do not exploit uncertainty feedback to guide data augmentation dynamically. Existing augmentation techniques are typically static or heuristic and fail to adaptively challenge the model on uncertain inputs to enhance calibration robustness.

APPROACH:  
We propose Uncertainty-Aware Data Augmentation (UADA), which uses predictive uncertainty scores computed per input (via entropy or mutual information from MC-Dropout sampling) during training to modulate augmentation strength and probability on-the-fly. Inputs with higher uncertainty receive stronger perturbations (e.g., larger rotations, brightness shifts), creating a feedback loop that prioritizes challenging samples. To mitigate computational overhead and stabilize training, uncertainty estimation is performed at configurable intervals with batch-level normalization and caching strategies. Ablations include random and heuristic adaptive augmentation schedules to isolate uncertainty-specific effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate UADA on CIFAR-10-C to stress-test calibration under common corruptions and on Medical MNIST to assess robustness in a high-stakes medical imaging domain. Baselines include standard augmentation training, MC-Dropout without adaptive augmentation, ensembles with standard augmentation, and non-uncertainty-driven adaptive augmentation controls. Metrics are Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL), and predictive accuracy on clean, corrupted, and out-of-distribution test sets. Success requires ≥10% statistically significant ECE reduction and ≥0.05 average NLL decrease over the best baseline, with accuracy degradation ≤1%.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work which either applies uncertainty estimation post hoc or uses static augmentation, UADA explicitly integrates uncertainty feedback into data augmentation, creating an adaptive curriculum that focuses training on uncertain samples to directly improve calibration. This approach bridges uncertainty quantification with augmentation-driven regularization, providing theoretical grounding beyond heuristic or hard-example mining methods while addressing computational challenges for practical deployment.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating and aggregating uncertainty estimates from multiple intermediate layers of deep neural networks via a learned fusion network improves predictive uncertainty calibration beyond output-layer-only uncertainty quantification methods.

BACKGROUND: Predictive uncertainty quantification (UQ) in deep neural networks remains a critical challenge, especially in safety-sensitive applications such as medical diagnosis and robustness-critical vision tasks. Existing techniques typically estimate uncertainty solely at the output softmax layer, potentially missing complementary information encoded in intermediate representations. There is limited understanding of whether leveraging multi-level uncertainty signals can meaningfully enhance calibration and robustness under distribution shifts.

APPROACH: We propose a novel framework that applies Monte Carlo Dropout at several intermediate ResNet-34 blocks to extract stochastic predictive distributions at multiple network depths. These per-layer uncertainties (e.g., variances and entropies) are normalized and concatenated, then fed into a small auxiliary neural network trained jointly with the classifier to produce a fused, improved uncertainty estimate. Training incorporates a differentiable calibration regularizer that encourages better alignment between predicted confidence and true correctness, contrasting with baseline methods that estimate uncertainty only at the output layer.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate predictive uncertainty calibration on CIFAR-10 (clean and CIFAR-10-C corruption benchmarks) and PathMNIST from the Medical MNIST dataset, measuring Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), and Brier score. Baselines include MC Dropout and Bayesian Neural Network uncertainty estimated solely at the output layer, as well as ablations with simple unweighted averaging of intermediate uncertainties and without the learned aggregator. The hypothesis will be falsified if the intermediate-layer fusion approach fails to improve ECE by at least 10% relative to the best output-layer baseline or degrades NLL and Brier scores on both in- and out-of-distribution datasets.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing exclusively on output-layer uncertainty, our method explicitly exploits complementary uncertainty signals from multiple intermediate layers via learned fusion with joint calibration optimization. This principled multi-level approach differentiates from ensemble or multi-layer Bayesian methods by integrating layer-wise stochasticity within a single end-to-end trainable framework, providing a theoretically motivated and empirically validated pathway to improved uncertainty calibration under domain shifts.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating learned data-dependent priors via hypernetworks conditioned on training data statistics into Bayesian neural networks improves uncertainty calibration more effectively than fixed Gaussian priors across diverse image classification benchmarks.

BACKGROUND: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) typically employ fixed, static priors on weights, which may inadequately capture dataset-specific characteristics and limit uncertainty calibration performance. Accurately calibrated uncertainty is critical for reliable model deployment in safety-sensitive applications, yet it remains an open challenge to design priors that adapt to data distributions without overfitting or sacrificing predictive accuracy.

APPROACH: We propose a hierarchical BNN framework wherein a hypernetwork generates weight priors conditioned on learned data embeddings summarizing training set statistics, enabling data-dependent adaptive priors. Training proceeds via variational inference with reparameterization gradients, rigorously controlling hypernetwork capacity and training protocols to isolate the effect of learned priors while matching computational budgets of baselines.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN against baselines including (1) fixed-prior BNNs with isotropic Gaussian priors, (2) Monte Carlo Dropout, and (3) deep ensembles. Key metrics comprise Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), classification accuracy, and extended robustness checks such as out-of-distribution detection, adversarial calibration, and dataset shift scenarios. Success is defined as consistent ≥10% relative reduction in ECE and statistically significant NLL improvements (p < 0.05) over fixed-prior BNNs without accuracy degradation.

NOVELTY: Unlike existing works that use static or heuristic priors, our method explicitly learns data-dependent hierarchical priors through a stable and constrained hypernetwork architecture, bridging a conceptual gap beyond empirical Bayes approaches. This enables principled adaptation to dataset-specific distributions while rigorously analyzing risks of overfitting and generalization under distributional shifts, providing a novel path to more reliable Bayesian uncertainty quantification in deep learning.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pre-trained on rigorously integrated multi-omics single-cell datasets—combining scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and single-cell methylation—achieve significantly improved cell-type-specific gene regulatory network prediction accuracy compared to single-modality models, as validated by cross-cell-type generalization against experimentally confirmed regulatory interactions.

BACKGROUND:  
Predicting gene regulatory networks (GRNs) at single-cell resolution remains a critical challenge due to the complex, multi-layered regulatory mechanisms that govern cellular identity and function. Existing models predominantly rely on single-modality data such as scRNA-seq, limiting their ability to capture epigenetic and chromatin context. Moreover, current GRN inference methods often lack scalability and robust validation against ground truth regulatory interactions derived from perturbation experiments or curated databases.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a multi-modal transformer-based foundation model architecture with modality-specific encoders and a shared latent space, pre-trained via self-supervised masked token prediction across integrated scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and methylation data from partially matched single-cell datasets (e.g., Human Cell Atlas PBMC multi-omics). To address data heterogeneity and scarcity, we will apply state-of-the-art computational alignment methods, data augmentation, and modality-shuffling ablations to isolate the benefit of true multi-modal integration. Comparative baseline models include single-modality foundation models (scBERT/scGPT for scRNA-seq, peak embedding transformers for scATAC-seq), and classical GRN inference methods (GENIE3, SCENIC).

EXPERIMENT:  
Model performance will be evaluated on held-out cell types by predicting regulatory edges benchmarked against experimentally validated interactions from DoRothEA and Perturb-seq datasets, using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and area under the ROC curve (AUROC) as primary metrics. Statistical significance of a minimum 10% relative improvement over the best single-modality baseline will be tested via paired bootstrap tests (p < 0.05). Additional validation includes orthogonal biological pathway enrichment analyses and interpretability assessments to link model predictions with mechanistic regulatory insights.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines a multi-modal foundation model pre-training framework with rigorous data integration strategies and comprehensive validation against perturbation-grounded regulatory networks, going beyond prior single-modality or protein interaction-focused models. It theoretically and empirically substantiates that joint modeling of expression, chromatin accessibility, and methylation at single-cell resolution enhances the fidelity and biological interpretability of cell-type-specific GRNs.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pre-trained on integrated multi-omics single-cell datasets combining transcriptomics and epigenomics outperform single-modality models in accurately predicting rare cell states across diverse human tissues.

BACKGROUND:  
Rare cell states, such as progenitor or rare immune subpopulations, are critical for understanding development and disease but are challenging to identify due to their low abundance and high biological variability. Existing single-cell models trained on single modalities (e.g., scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq alone) often lack sufficient power and robustness to generalize rare cell state predictions across tissues. Leveraging multi-omics data integration in foundation models may provide richer, complementary biological context, improving sensitivity and specificity in rare cell classification.

APPROACH:  
We propose a transformer-based foundation model architecture with modality-specific encoders for gene expression and chromatin accessibility, integrated via cross-modal attention to learn unified cellular embeddings. The model will be pre-trained on large-scale unlabeled multi-omics datasets using self-supervised tasks (masked token prediction and cross-modal contrastive learning) to capture cross-modality biological signals. Fine-tuning will target supervised rare cell state classification on held-out tissues, with rigorous controls including batch correction, domain adaptation, and comparison against matched single-modality foundation models and simpler multi-omics baselines.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be trained and evaluated on publicly available multi-omics single-cell datasets, specifically the Human Cell Atlas multi-omics compendium (paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq across multiple human tissues) and the 10x Genomics Multiome dataset (PBMC and bone marrow samples). Baselines include scRNA-seq-only and scATAC-seq-only foundation models with identical architectures, as well as early fusion and feature concatenation multi-omics baselines. Performance will be measured by area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and F1-score on rare cell states defined by <1% population frequency, with statistical power analyses ensuring sufficient representation. The hypothesis will be supported if the multi-omics model improves AUPRC by ≥10% relative to the best single-modality model; failure to exceed both single-modality models by ≥5% will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates multi-omics single-cell data through a cross-modal attention foundation model architecture explicitly designed to enhance rare cell state prediction, addressing limitations of prior single-modality and simpler fusion approaches. By combining rigorous power analysis, confounder controls, and realistic performance thresholds grounded in diverse human tissue datasets, our approach advances both theoretical understanding and practical capabilities in multi-modal single-cell biology.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained jointly on human genomic sequences and single-cell transcriptomic profiles with linked chromatin accessibility data will predict cell-type-specific regulatory element activity with significantly higher accuracy than unimodal models trained on either data type alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately predicting cell-type-specific regulatory element activity remains a fundamental challenge in genomics, complicated by the complex interplay between DNA sequence and cell-type context reflected in gene expression. Existing models primarily leverage either genomic sequence data or transcriptomic profiles in isolation, limiting their ability to capture complementary regulatory signals. Integrating multi-omics data, particularly single-cell transcriptomics coupled with chromatin accessibility, offers a promising avenue to improve predictive modeling of regulatory activity across diverse human cell types.

APPROACH:  
We propose a multimodal foundation model employing a dual-encoder transformer architecture with cross-modal attention layers that fuse embeddings from genomic sequences and single-cell transcriptomic data linked via scATAC-seq peak-gene associations. The model will be pretrained using a contrastive learning objective that aligns regulatory sequences with cognate cell-type expression profiles, followed by fine-tuning to predict regulatory activity labels derived from ENCODE DNase hypersensitivity and TF ChIP-seq peak data. Comparative baselines will include a unimodal sequence-only transformer (similar to Enformer) and a unimodal expression-only graph neural network.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be trained and evaluated on matched human datasets: ENCODE Phase 3 for genomic regulatory element annotations, and Human Cell Atlas single-cell RNA-seq and scATAC-seq multimodal datasets for transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility information across diverse cell types. Performance will be measured on held-out cell types and regulatory regions using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and area under the ROC curve (AUROC). Statistical significance of improvements (≥5% absolute AUPRC gain) will be confirmed via bootstrap resampling and power analysis. Ablation studies and randomized modality pairing controls will isolate the contribution of multimodal integration.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior unimodal or simplistic multimodal models by explicitly leveraging single-cell multimodal data for high-confidence cell-type-specific regulatory label generation and employing a novel contrastive pretraining framework with cross-modal attention to deeply integrate sequence and expression modalities. The systematic incorporation of rigorous controls, ablation experiments, and statistical power analysis ensures robust attribution of predictive gains to the multimodal foundation model, setting a new standard for cell-type-resolved regulatory genomics modeling.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained on large-scale, cell-type-matched single-cell multi-omics data can more accurately predict cell-type-specific enhancer-gene regulatory interactions than models pretrained on bulk tissue data, as validated by CRISPR perturbation datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately linking enhancers to their target genes in a cell-type-specific manner remains a major challenge in genomics due to cellular heterogeneity and context-dependent regulatory mechanisms. Bulk tissue data aggregate signals from diverse cell types, often obscuring these specific interactions. Leveraging foundation models pretrained on single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data offers the potential to capture fine-grained regulatory relationships that are invisible in bulk profiles.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a transformer-based multi-modal foundation model that jointly embeds paired single-cell chromatin accessibility and gene expression data from the Human Cell Atlas, carefully subsetted to match the cell types of CRISPR validation studies (e.g., K562, GM12878). The model will be pretrained using masked token prediction to learn contextual regulatory features and then fine-tuned to predict enhancer-gene interactions, employing rigorously curated negative samples that account for cell-type-specific chromatin context and genomic properties. A comparable architecture will be trained on aggregated bulk data from GTEx for direct performance comparison.

EXPERIMENT:  
Prediction accuracy will be evaluated on held-out enhancer-gene pairs experimentally validated by large-scale CRISPR perturbation screens (Fulco et al., 2019; Gasperini et al., 2019) using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Statistical significance will be assessed over multiple random seeds and cross-validation folds, with a ≥5% absolute increase in AUPR compared to bulk-trained models considered support for the hypothesis. Failure to achieve this or a consistent >3% decrease will falsify it.

NOVELTY:  
This work differentiates itself by explicitly aligning single-cell pretraining data with the exact cell lines used for experimental validation, implementing biologically informed negative sampling strategies, and rigorously quantifying the practical advantage of single-cell foundation models over bulk-trained counterparts for enhancer-gene prediction—an advance beyond prior bulk-focused or unaligned approaches in the literature.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Pretraining transformer-based foundation models on harmonized single-cell transcriptomic data from multiple species, using rigorously curated ortholog gene vocabularies, will improve the accuracy and generalizability of cell-type-specific gene regulatory network (GRN) prediction compared to species-specific models.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell transcriptomes is critical for understanding cell identity and function, but existing models trained on single-species data often fail to capture conserved regulatory mechanisms and generalize poorly to novel cell types. Leveraging shared regulatory logic across species via foundation models pretrained on large multi-species datasets remains an open challenge, complicated by ortholog mapping, data heterogeneity, and the lack of robust multi-species evaluation frameworks.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a transformer-based foundation model pretrained with masked gene expression modeling over a combined multi-species single-cell RNA-seq dataset (Tabula Muris for mouse, Human Cell Atlas lung and immune subsets, and zebrafish embryogenesis from Single Cell Expression Atlas), using a rigorously benchmarked ortholog mapping pipeline to construct a shared gene vocabulary. Fine-tuning will incorporate a graph neural network head that integrates learned embeddings with cell-type labels to predict regulatory edges, with ablation and negative control experiments including models trained without ortholog mapping and shuffled data baselines.

EXPERIMENT:  
Model performance will be evaluated on held-out test sets of cell-type-specific regulatory interactions from curated sources—CellNet for human and mouse, and perturbation-inferred zebrafish GRNs—using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and area under the ROC curve (AUROC), alongside leave-one-cell-type-out validation to assess generalization. Statistical comparisons (paired t-tests across cell types, p < 0.05) and >5% absolute AUPR improvement over species-specific baselines will constitute evidence supporting the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines rigorous ortholog curation and batch-corrected multi-species single-cell transcriptomes to pretrain foundation models explicitly designed for cross-species regulatory inference, integrating a graph neural network fine-tuning framework, which together surpass prior multi-species or multi-modal single-cell models focused primarily on co-expression or annotation transfer rather than direct GRN prediction and generalizability to unseen cell types.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Agents that dynamically adapt their communication signaling frequency based on reliably estimated task complexity in multi-agent reinforcement learning environments with distinct complexity phases achieve superior trade-offs between collective task success and communication overhead compared to fixed-rate or heuristic-based communication, provided that a communication stability regularizer ensures smooth frequency modulation.

BACKGROUND:  
Effective communication in multi-agent systems is critical for coordinated task performance but often incurs high overhead when performed at fixed or heuristic-driven rates. Existing adaptive communication approaches primarily rely on uncertainty or novelty signals without formally leveraging task complexity estimations, leading to suboptimal trade-offs and unstable communication patterns. This research addresses the gap of principled, complexity-driven dynamic communication frequency modulation with formal stability guarantees in multi-agent reinforcement learning contexts featuring distinct environmental complexity phases.

APPROACH:  
We introduce a complexity-adaptive communication controller integrated into each agent’s policy, where a learned complexity estimator module predicts a continuous task complexity score from environment state features (e.g., entropy, obstacles, progress). This score modulates the communication signaling probability, increasing frequency during high complexity and reducing it during low complexity phases. A communication stability regularizer penalizes abrupt frequency changes, ensuring temporal smoothness. Agents are trained end-to-end using PPO with a composite reward balancing collective task success and communication cost. Rigorous offline validation of the complexity estimator and ablation of stability mechanisms are conducted to isolate their effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Experiments begin with a controlled environment exhibiting well-defined complexity phases to tune and validate the complexity estimator and stability controls, then extend to the MineRL BASALT benchmark and Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) with custom low- and high-complexity scenarios. Baselines include fixed-rate communication agents, heuristic-based adaptive communicators, and no-communication agents. Metrics are Collective Task Success Rate (CTSR), Communication Overhead Ratio (COR), and the composite Communication Efficiency Index (CEI = CTSR / COR). Statistical tests (p<0.05) determine whether adaptive-frequency agents outperform baselines by at least 10% in CEI without unstable communication patterns.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely formalizes the use of continuous task complexity estimation for dynamic communication frequency modulation in multi-agent systems, accompanied by a theoretically motivated communication stability regularizer to prevent oscillations. Unlike prior methods based on uncertainty or novelty, it provides a principled framework with offline estimator validation, ablation of stability mechanisms, and theoretical analysis of adaptation stability and convergence under noisy, non-stationary conditions, advancing beyond heuristic or fixed scheduling approaches in emergent communication research.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems employing a meta-controller-driven dynamic role-switching communication protocol that adapts to network disruptions will achieve significantly more robust coordination and task performance than fixed-role or adaptive-but-static communication schemas.

BACKGROUND:  
Robust emergent communication in multi-agent systems remains a critical challenge, especially under realistic network impairments such as message loss and latency. Existing methods predominantly rely on fixed communication roles or static adaptation policies, limiting agents’ ability to flexibly reassign communication responsibilities in response to varying network conditions and task demands. This gap impedes robustness and efficiency in coordination under partial observability and noisy communication channels.

APPROACH:  
We propose a Dynamic Role-Switching Communication (DRS-Comm) architecture featuring a hierarchical meta-controller neural network that integrates local agent observations, recent communication success metrics, and task progress indicators to dynamically assign communication roles (sender, receiver, coordinator) every N timesteps. Role-switching policies are jointly trained with the agents’ task policies using a multi-agent actor-critic algorithm (MAPPO) under stochastic simulated network disruptions (random message dropouts and delays up to 40% packet loss), enabling proactive adaptation of communication strategies to maintain coordination robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate DRS-Comm on two benchmark multi-agent environments: Google Research Football (continuous, physics-based coordination) and StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge (discrete, heterogeneous agents with strategic roles). Baselines include no-communication, random communication, fixed-role communication trained with and without network disruptions, and adaptive communication without role-switching. Metrics are task completion rate, average episode reward, and communication quality measured by successful message delivery rate and information entropy of messages. Statistical significance is assessed via paired t-tests (p < 0.05) across multiple disruption levels (0%, 20%, 40% packet loss). Ablations explore role-switching frequency and meta-controller design variants.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior works that fix communication roles or adapt communication parameters statically, DRS-Comm introduces a learnable hierarchical meta-controller enabling dynamic role reassignment conditioned on network state and task context, rigorously integrating communication robustness theory with reinforcement learning. The inclusion of expanded baselines and theoretically motivated metrics isolates the unique contribution of dynamic role-switching to emergent communication resilience under realistic network impairments.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems that employ explicitly defined and rigorously validated dynamic role-switching mechanisms between sender and receiver agents develop more efficient and generalizable emergent communication protocols than systems with fixed sender-receiver roles.

BACKGROUND:  
Current emergent communication research largely assumes static sender-receiver roles, which may limit the efficiency and adaptability of learned languages. However, the causal impact of role dynamics on communication efficiency, language compositionality, and generalization remains underexplored, especially when controlling for architectural symmetries and parameter sharing. Addressing this gap is crucial to understanding how role flexibility influences coordination and language evolution in multi-agent systems.

APPROACH:  
We propose a controlled comparison between two multi-agent system variants trained on the Multi-Agent Particle Environment’s speaker-listener navigation task and the SCONE grounded language dataset: (1) a dynamic-role system with two distinct switching schemes—a fixed periodic swap every N episodes validated by preliminary stability analyses, and a learned meta-controller network trained to assign roles adaptively; and (2) a fixed-role system with static sender and receiver assignments. Both systems employ identical LSTM-based architectures with parameter sharing carefully isolated via ablation studies to disentangle the effects of role-switching from model symmetry.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate communication efficiency using task success rate (target >90%), average message length, and mutual information between messages and environment states estimated via bias-controlled neural estimators, alongside generalization accuracy on unseen SCONE compositional instructions (≥10% above chance). Statistical significance is assessed across five independent runs with matched model capacities and training regimes, and ablations isolate the contribution of switching frequency and meta-controller learning to observed effects.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously defines and validates dynamic role-switching mechanisms with feasibility analyses and causal controls, providing the first falsifiable, theoretically motivated empirical test of role dynamics on emergent communication efficiency, compositionality, and generalization—advancing beyond prior fixed-role or parameter-sharing assumptions typical in emergent language research.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Multi-agent systems employing dynamic, context-dependent communication protocols achieve significantly better coordination and communication efficiency than fixed-protocol or no-communication systems in uncertain, complex environments.

BACKGROUND: Coordinated multi-agent decision-making under environmental uncertainty remains a critical challenge, particularly in domains requiring flexible and scalable communication strategies. While fixed communication protocols have been standard, their rigidity limits adaptability to changing contexts; thus, it remains an open problem whether adaptive communication protocols can consistently improve coordination performance and communication efficiency in stochastic, partially observable settings.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework where agents use learned context encoders to generate latent embeddings from local and global observations, conditioning a dynamically adaptive communication policy that modulates message content and timing. This dynamic communication protocol (DCP) is compared against fixed communication protocol (FCP) agents—sharing identical base architectures but restricted to static message vocabularies—and no-communication (NC) agents to isolate the impact of communication adaptivity.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate all agent types on benchmark coordination tasks with tunable environmental uncertainty in the Google Research Football (GRF) environment and the StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). Performance metrics include task completion rate, average cumulative reward, and communication efficiency—quantified both by normalized message volume and mutual information between messages and task-relevant states—across 30 independent runs per condition. Statistical significance testing (p < 0.05) will confirm if DCP agents outperform FCP agents under high uncertainty, falsifying the hypothesis if no difference or FCP superiority is observed.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that either assumes fixed communication protocols or explores emergent communication without rigorous uncertainty control, our approach explicitly formalizes and operationalizes communication adaptivity, introduces quantitative uncertainty modulation, and integrates information-theoretic metrics for communication efficiency. This comprehensive framework enables the first systematic empirical test of dynamic communication advantages in complex, stochastic MAS benchmarks.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Incorporating controlled intermittent communication dropout during training combined with a variational mutual information-based redundancy incentive will induce robust, semantically meaningful emergent communication protocols in multi-agent systems without significant task performance loss under unreliable channels.

BACKGROUND: Multi-agent systems often rely on communication protocols that degrade sharply under realistic conditions of intermittent message loss, limiting their applicability in noisy or bandwidth-constrained environments. Prior work typically overlooks systematic robustness training and explicit incentives for temporal redundancy, which may be key to developing communication that tolerates channel unreliability while maintaining task effectiveness.

APPROACH: We propose training agents with stochastic communication dropout applied intermittently (e.g., 20% per timestep) alongside an auxiliary loss that encourages temporal redundancy by maximizing a tractable variational lower bound on mutual information between consecutive messages within each agent’s communication stream. This redundancy loss is carefully controlled to avoid trivial repetition by penalizing message entropy inflation, and is jointly optimized with the main task reward using PPO in recurrent policy networks.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on the StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) and the Google Research Football Environment under partial observability, comparing (1) a vanilla baseline without dropout or redundancy incentives, (2) dropout-only, (3) redundancy-only, and (4) the combined method. Robustness is tested by measuring task performance and communication efficiency across a spectrum of dropout patterns—including i.i.d. and bursty correlated dropouts—from 0% to 50% at test time, with success defined as at least 10% improvement in average win rate or goals scored over all baselines under high-dropout conditions and less than 15% relative performance degradation compared to no-dropout tests.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior studies that either neglect robustness or impose inductive biases on communication structure, our method rigorously integrates scalable variational mutual information estimation to incentivize meaningful temporal redundancy and systematically evaluates robustness across realistic dropout regimes, empirically validating and theoretically motivating the critical role of redundancy in emergent multi-agent communication under unreliable channels.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether specific attention heads in multilingual transformer models mechanistically encode universal compositional syntactic rules by demonstrating consistent, causally grounded head-function mappings that generalize across typologically diverse languages.

BACKGROUND:  
While attention patterns in transformer models have been correlated with syntactic structures, it remains unclear if these patterns reflect mechanistic, compositional syntactic rules that are language-universal or merely statistical associations. Prior monolingual probing studies and correlational analyses do not establish causal roles of attention heads or their cross-lingual consistency, leaving an open problem in mechanistic interpretability and the universality of syntactic representations in multilingual models.

APPROACH:  
We will identify attention heads in pretrained multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-R) that robustly predict syntactic dependencies within individual languages by combining attention alignment metrics with causal interventions such as targeted head ablations and synthetic attention rewiring. We then assess cross-lingual generalization by comparing head-syntactic function mappings across English, Finnish, and Japanese UD treebanks using canonical correlation analysis (CCA/SVCCA) on aligned attention patterns with careful preprocessing to normalize tokenization and morphology effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using Universal Dependencies datasets for English, Finnish, and Japanese, we measure Attention Head Accuracy (AHA) as the fraction of tokens whose highest-attention corresponds to their syntactic head, requiring cross-lingual AHA >70% and CCA similarity >0.75 to confirm shared head roles. Controlled baselines include random head assignments, monolingual syntactic probes, and finetuned syntactic classifiers. Ablation studies will test causal necessity of identified heads, while failure to find consistent cross-lingual alignments or causal effects (AHA <50%, CCA <0.4) falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This approach advances mechanistic interpretability by integrating causal intervention methods with cross-lingual syntactic probing to rigorously test universality of attention-head syntactic roles, moving beyond purely correlational monolingual studies. It provides the first comprehensive, causally grounded evaluation of whether transformer attention heads encode truly compositional, language-general syntactic rules across typologically diverse languages.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
We propose to rigorously test the hypothesis that transformer language models internally implement distinct, causally independent algorithmic submodules corresponding to specific linguistic phenomena by identifying, ablating, and measuring isolated circuit function across multiple benchmarks.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations to understand how models represent and process linguistic information. While prior work has found evidence of circuits associated with linguistic behaviors, most transformer representations appear distributed and overlapping, challenging claims of strict modularity. A formal, quantitative test of whether submodules can be independently manipulated without collateral effects remains an open problem.

APPROACH:  
We will leverage causal mediation techniques, specifically activation patching, to identify neuron groups and attention heads causally critical for three well-defined linguistic phenomena—subject-verb agreement, coreference resolution, and negation understanding—in a pretrained GPT-2 Medium model. By ablating these identified sub-circuits individually at inference time and evaluating the resulting impact on all three corresponding tasks, we aim to formally assess the degree of functional modularity and independence among these submodules.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using SyntaxGym’s number agreement suite, the GAP coreference dataset, and GLUE Contrast Sets for negation, we will measure task-specific accuracy and F1 scores before and after targeted ablations. A successful demonstration of modularity requires a >20% relative performance drop on the ablated linguistic task with <5% relative degradation on the others, thereby falsifying overlapping distributed representations. Control experiments will ablate non-critical circuits to validate specificity.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior interpretability studies that largely provide descriptive circuit analyses or focus on single phenomena, our work introduces a formal, quantitative causal framework to identify and independently manipulate linguistic submodules, rigorously testing mechanistic modularity in transformer LMs. This bridges a critical gap by proposing explicit, falsifiable criteria for modularity and addressing partial overlaps through rigorous causal effect decomposition rather than heuristic or correlational methods alone.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Systematically test whether individual transformer attention heads implement modular mechanistic subroutines by employing rigorously validated causal interventions—activation patching and ablations—combined with multi-head and multi-condition controls to measure their isolated effect on task-specific performance.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer the internal computations of transformer models by identifying discrete components responsible for specific functions. A central open question is whether individual attention heads correspond to modular subroutines that can be toggled on or off without degrading overall model performance on targeted linguistic tasks. Existing work often relies on correlational heuristics and single-head ablations, leaving unresolved whether these components are truly mechanistically modular or entangled and distributed.

APPROACH:  
We first develop a rigorous, multi-modal candidate head identification pipeline combining theory-driven hypotheses, causal probing, and prior interpretability findings to validate heads purportedly encoding mechanistic subroutines (e.g., coreference tracking). Then, we perform fine-grained causal interventions: selective activation patching and zeroing of individual and combinations of heads during inference on task-relevant inputs, alongside rich control interventions that include random-head patching and whole-layer ablations. This approach accounts for distributed redundancy and compensatory dynamics to robustly infer the causal contribution of candidate heads.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on two carefully selected benchmarks—HellaSwag for commonsense and narrative reasoning, and the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC) for coreference resolution—measuring absolute task accuracy changes under intervention. We define mechanistic modularity as the ability to fully activate or deactivate a candidate head with less than 1% accuracy drop, and falsify it if any candidate head’s patching or ablation causes a statistically significant accuracy reduction of 5% or more compared to the baseline and random-patching controls.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior correlational and single-head ablation analyses by combining multi-modal candidate validation, combinatorial causal interventions, and rigorous controls that explicitly address distributed and compensatory model behaviors. It provides a principled, falsifiable test of mechanistic modularity in transformer attention heads, thus sharpening the theoretical framing and empirical rigor of mechanistic interpretability studies.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Analyzing intermediate attention heads conditioned on task-specific probing datasets significantly improves the accuracy of mechanistic circuit identification in transformer models compared to analyses performed on generic linguistic corpora.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer the internal computations of transformer models by identifying circuits that implement specific behaviors. However, existing approaches primarily analyze models on generic corpora, which may obscure task-relevant circuits due to distributed and entangled representations. Establishing whether conditioning interpretability analyses on carefully chosen, well-structured probing datasets clarifies circuit discovery remains an open challenge.

APPROACH:  
We propose to apply conditional activation patching focused on intermediate attention heads in transformer models fine-tuned on task-specific datasets with known algorithmic structure, such as the Colored MNIST Visual Reasoning dataset (adapted for vision transformers) and the CFQ semantic parsing dataset. By comparing circuit identification precision and recall against known ground-truth circuits on these probing datasets versus a generic corpus baseline (WikiText-103), we quantify interpretability gains attributable to task conditioning.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using a GPT-2 medium model fine-tuned separately on each dataset, we replicate and extend recent mechanistic interpretability pipelines involving activation patching and causal mediation on both generic and task-specific inputs.
